messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael, thank you for your quick response. I have run this model with and without the 'dead absorbing' state in the m-array format and the results are the same. I tested that again this morning by running the model with and without the dead absorbing state with CMRR data for all years and there were no estimation issues in either example. However, when there are only recoveries for a period of time between CMR surveys the estimation issue (bias in recovery probability + survival) remains regardless of the additional dead state. This issue does not occur when running the same data through the state-space format.

I am wondering if anyone else has experience running CMRR models when there are some years with CMR and years with recoveries only but analyzed in the m-array format. Or, if anyone knows whether the m-array code needs to be adapted within jags to deal with such a scenario. I have two projects that would greatly benefit from the time saved using the m-array over the state-space format so I would love to figure this out! Thank you!

On Tuesday, September 1, 2020 at 12:31:33 AM UTC-6 Schaub Michael wrote:
> Hi Kylee,
>
> When you formulate a multistate model that jointly analyses live recaptures and dead recoveries, you need to include 2 death states (recently dead and long-time dead). The latter is absorbing and non-observable. It is needed, because otherwise a dead individual can be repeatedly be recovered. See Chapter 9.5 in the BPA book.
>
> Best wishes
>
> Michael
>
> Von: hmec...@googlegroups.com [hmec...@googlegroups.com]" im Auftrag von "Kylee Dunham [kdu...@ualberta.ca]
> Gesendet: Freitag, 28. August 2020 00:07
> An: hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology
> Betreff: estimation issues with multistate m-array in jags
>
> Hello,
>
> I am having some trouble with a joint analysis of live recapture and dead recovery data using a multi-state m-array format in JAGs. I am running simulations based on an “ideal” data set that includes CMR and recoveries every year – and in this case the code works without a problem and the posteriors include truth. Therefore, I know this code is working. However, I am trying to fit the model based on data similar to data scenario which includes 3 years of CMR+recoveries followed by 9 years with recoveries only followed by 2 years of CMR+recoveries (i.e., dead recoveries are recorded in every year of the study but capture-mark-recapture surveys only occur in the first 3 years and the last 2 years of the study). I can fit these data in JAGs using the state-space format and the estimates are fine. But when I try to fit these data in JAGs using the m-array format the estimates are biased (high or low depends on the parameter). This leads me to believe there is something about the code within JAGs that is causing this issue, but I am not certain.
>
>
>
> Has anyone else run into this problem before? I have included my code and would appreciate any help you can provide!
>

>

>

>
> marked <- matrix(0, ncol = n.states, nrow = n.occasions)
>

>
>   marked[t,1] <- 100
>
> }
>
> marked[4:12,1] <- 0 # no individuals released or recaptured in these years
>
>
> totrel <- sum(marked) * (n.occasions-1)
>

>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Again,

Thanks for all the comments that helped me get my model up and running. After some trial and error with priors and initial values, I have managed to produce what seems like reasonable estimates. However, I am hoping for some clarification on interpretation and extending the model. I have not provided any indexing on K, r, or p for my previous model. Therefore, should I interpret these parameters as mean estimates for the entire population of plots and not as per plot estimates? If I am correct, I would like to extend the model by adding some covariates on at least K and p for plot specific estimates, which I am also hoping will improve the precision of those estimates.

Unfortunately, I seem to be struggling to get that model to run with parent node inconsistency errors. Below is my model call to JAGS and init value specifications. Any tips or further thoughts on getting this model up and running. I have read that it can be challenging to specify these initial values and fit these models. Do I just need more trial and error?

Thanks,

Matt

str(abdu_data <- list(y = data_matrix, nsites = nrow(data_matrix),
                  nyears = ncol(data_matrix), phen=phen, lakea=lakea)) # note length added

# Specify model in BUGS language

sink("gompertz_p_covs")
cat("
model {
# Priors
lambda ~ dunif(0,100) # Abundance
K0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01) # Carrying Capacity
K1 ~ dnorm(0,0.01)
r0 ~ dnorm(0,0.01)
p0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
p1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
iota ~ dunif(0,25) #Immigration
#p ~ dunif(0.05,0.95)

# Likelihood
for(i in 1:nsites){
   # State process: initial condition
   N[i,1] ~ dpois(lambda)

   # State process: transition model
   for(t in 1:(nyears-1)){

      r[i,t] <- exp(r0)

      K[i,t] <- exp(K0 + K1*lakea[i,t])

      muN[i,t] <- N[i,t] * exp(r[i,t] * (1 - log(N[i,t] + 1) / log(K[i,t] + 1))) + iota

      N[i,t+1] ~ dpois(muN[i,t])

   }

   # Observation process
   for(t in 1:nyears){

      logit(p[i,t]) <- p0 + p1*phen[i,t]
      y[i,t] ~ dbin(p[i,t], N[i,t])
      }
}

# Derived quantities

}
")
sink()

#Starting N
Nst <- array(NA, dim = dim(data_matrix))

tmp <- apply(data_matrix, 1, max, na.rm = TRUE)
tmp[tmp == '-Inf'] <- 2
Nst[,1] <- tmp

# Initial values
inits2 <- function(){list(N=Nst+25, r0 = rnorm(1), lambda=runif(1, 5, 20),
                          K0=rnorm(1), K1=rnorm(1), iota=rnorm(1),
                          p0=rnorm(1), p1=rnorm(1))}

# Parameters monitored
params2 <-c("K", "N", "r", "p")

# MCMC settings
na <- 10 ; ni <- 1000 ; nt <- 10 ; nb <- 100 ; nc <- 3 #reduced just to get model running

# try different seeds in hopes of getting one that runs
set.seed(299, kind = "Mersenne-Twister")

gomp_jags_covs <- jags(abdu_data, inits2, params2, "gompertz_p_covs",

                  n.adapt = na, n.chains = nc,
                  n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni, n.burnin = nb, parallel = TRUE)

print(gomp_jags_covs)
traceplot(gomp_jags_covs)

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm trying to run a multistate Jolly-Seber model in JAGS using Kéry & Schaub BPA. To start, I simply copied the BPA JAGS code <https://www.vogelwarte.ch/assets/files/publications/BPA/BPA%20with%20JAGS.txt>, specifically 1) the model under section 10.3.2, 2) the data generation code under section 10.4, and 3) the code to run the model under 10.4.2.

When I run this code, I get the following error after running JAGS:

"Error in setParameters(init.values[[i]], i) : Error in node po[1,1,1,2]
Cannot set value of non-variable node"

FYI, when I do the same for the restricted occupancy and superpopulation parameterisations, the models run just fine. I do actually need to use the multistate formulation because the model will later be expanded to include multiple disease states. Can anyone clarify what's going on?

Looking forward to your answers. :)

Kind regards,
Matt Hollanders

# 10.3.2. The JS model as a multistate model
# Specify model in BUGS language

   phi[t] <- mean.phi

   p[t] <- mean.p
   }

mean.phi ~ dunif(0, 1)    # Prior for mean survival
mean.p ~ dunif(0, 1)      # Prior for mean capture

# Define state-transition and observation matrices
for (i in 1:M){
   # Define probabilities of state S(t+1) given S(t)
   for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
      ps[1,i,t,1] <- 1-gamma[t]
      ps[1,i,t,2] <- gamma[t]
      ps[1,i,t,3] <- 0
      ps[2,i,t,1] <- 0
      ps[2,i,t,2] <- phi[t]
      ps[2,i,t,3] <- 1-phi[t]
      ps[3,i,t,1] <- 0
      ps[3,i,t,2] <- 0
      ps[3,i,t,3] <- 1

      # Define probabilities of O(t) given S(t)
      po[1,i,t,1] <- 0
      po[1,i,t,2] <- 1
      po[2,i,t,1] <- p[t]
      po[2,i,t,2] <- 1-p[t]
      po[3,i,t,1] <- 0
      po[3,i,t,2] <- 1
      } #t
   } #i

# Likelihood
for (i in 1:M){
   # Define latent state at first occasion
   z[i,1] <- 1   # Make sure that all M individuals are in state 1 at t=1
   for (t in 2:n.occasions){
      # State process: draw S(t) given S(t-1)
      z[i,t] ~ dcat(ps[z[i,t-1], i, t-1,])
      # Observation process: draw O(t) given S(t)
      y[i,t] ~ dcat(po[z[i,t], i, t-1,])
      } #t
   } #i

# Calculate derived population parameters
for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
   qgamma[t] <- 1-gamma[t]
   }
cprob[1] <- gamma[1]
for (t in 2:(n.occasions-1)){
   cprob[t] <- gamma[t] * prod(qgamma[1:(t-1)])
   } #t
psi <- sum(cprob[])            # Inclusion probability
for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
   b[t] <- cprob[t] / psi      # Entry probability
   } #t

for (i in 1:M){
   for (t in 2:n.occasions){
      al[i,t-1] <- equals(z[i,t], 2)
      } #t
   for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
      d[i,t] <- equals(z[i,t]-al[i,t],0)
      } #t
   alive[i] <- sum(al[i,])
   } #i

for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
   N[t] <- sum(al[,t])        # Actual population size
   B[t] <- sum(d[,t])         # Number of entries
   } #t
for (i in 1:M){
   w[i] <- 1-equals(alive[i],0)
   } #i
Nsuper <- sum(w[])            # Superpopulation size
}
",fill = TRUE)
sink()

# 10.4. Models with constant survival and time-dependent entry
# Define parameter values
n.occasions <- 7                         # Number of capture occasions
N <- 400                                 # Superpopulation size
phi <- rep(0.7, n.occasions-1)           # Survival probabilities
b <- c(0.34, rep(0.11, n.occasions-1))   # Entry probabilities
p <- rep(0.5, n.occasions)               # Capture probabilities

PHI <- matrix(rep(phi, (n.occasions-1)*N), ncol = n.occasions-1, nrow = N, byrow = T)
P <- matrix(rep(p, n.occasions*N), ncol = n.occasions, nrow = N, byrow = T)

# Function to simulate capture-recapture data under the JS model
simul.js <- function(PHI, P, b, N){
  B <- rmultinom(1, N, b) # Generate no. of entering ind. per occasion
  n.occasions <- dim(PHI)[2] + 1
  CH.sur <- CH.p <- matrix(0, ncol = n.occasions, nrow = N)
  # Define a vector with the occasion of entering the population
  ent.occ <- numeric()
  for (t in 1:n.occasions){
    ent.occ <- c(ent.occ, rep(t, B[t]))
  }
  # Simulating survival
  for (i in 1:N){
    CH.sur[i, ent.occ[i]] <- 1   # Write 1 when ind. enters the pop.
    if (ent.occ[i] == n.occasions) next
    for (t in (ent.occ[i]+1):n.occasions){
      # Bernoulli trial: has individual survived occasion?
      sur <- rbinom(1, 1, PHI[i,t-1])
      ifelse (sur==1, CH.sur[i,t] <- 1, break)
    } #t
  } #i
  # Simulating capture
  for (i in 1:N){
    CH.p[i,] <- rbinom(n.occasions, 1, P[i,])
  } #i
  # Full capture-recapture matrix
  CH <- CH.sur * CH.p

  # Remove individuals never captured
  cap.sum <- rowSums(CH)
  never <- which(cap.sum == 0)
  CH <- CH[-never,]
  Nt <- colSums(CH.sur)    # Actual population size
  return(list(CH=CH, B=B, N=Nt))
}

# Execute simulation function
sim <- simul.js(PHI, P, b, N)
CH <- sim$CH

# 10.4.2 Analysis of the JS model as a multistate model
# Add dummy occasion
CH.du <- cbind(rep(0, dim(CH)[1]), CH)

# Augment data
nz <- 500
CH.ms <- rbind(CH.du, matrix(0, ncol = dim(CH.du)[2], nrow = nz))

# Recode CH matrix: a 0 is not allowed in WinBUGS!
CH.ms[CH.ms==0] <- 2                     # Not seen = 2, seen = 1

# Bundle data
jags.data <- list(y = CH.ms, n.occasions = dim(CH.ms)[2], M = dim(CH.ms)[1])

# Initial values
# As always in JAGS, good initial values need to be specified for the latent state z. They need to correspond to the true state, which is not the same as the observed state. Thus, we have given initial values of "1" for the latend state at all places before an individual was observed, an initial value of "2" at all places when the individual was observed alive or known to be alive and an initial value of "3" at all places after the last observation. The folllowing function creates the initial values.

js.multistate.init <- function(ch, nz){
  ch[ch==2] <- NA
  state <- ch
  for (i in 1:nrow(ch)){
    n1 <- min(which(ch[i,]==1))
    n2 <- max(which(ch[i,]==1))
    state[i,n1:n2] <- 2
  }
  state[state==0] <- NA
  get.first <- function(x) min(which(!is.na <http://is.na>(x)))
  get.last <- function(x) max(which(!is.na <http://is.na>(x)))
  f <- apply(state, 1, get.first)
  l <- apply(state, 1, get.last)
  for (i in 1:nrow(ch)){
    state[i,1:f[i]] <- 1
    if(l[i]!=ncol(ch)) state[i, (l[i]+1):ncol(ch)] <- 3
    state[i, f[i]] <- 2
  }
  state <- rbind(state, matrix(1, ncol = ncol(ch), nrow = nz))
  return(state)
}

inits <- function(){list(mean.phi = runif(1, 0, 1), mean.p = runif(1, 0, 1), z = js.multistate.init(CH.du, nz))}

# Parameters monitored
parameters <- c("mean.p", "mean.phi", "b", "Nsuper", "N", "B")

# MCMC settings
ni <- 20000
nt <- 3
nb <- 5000
nc <- 3

# Call JAGS from R (BRT 32 min)
js.ms <http://js.ms> <- jags(jags.data, inits, parameters, "js-ms.jags", n.chains = nc, n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni, n.burnin = nb)

messages.subject: A question on predator-prey interactions from multi-species occupancy models
messages.subject_clean: A question on predator-prey interactions from multi-species occupancy models
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!

I hope you are all doing healthy and safe!

I applied single-season, multi-species models to different pairs of predator-prey species detected in our camera-trapping surveys in northwestern Anatolia. I am trying to find out co-occurrence patterns and seasonality effects on them. I used Richmond-Waddle parametrization which is putting the true occupancy of a species as a covariate on the other one, so you will see the effects of presence/absence of one species to another. According to the terminology we define prey species as dominant and predator species as subordinate. I modeled the effects of prey species' presence/absence on the predator.

For the lynx (Lynx lynx) Eurasian hare (Lepus europaeus) pair, I got a bit confused from my results. Here you see the number of sites with each state of the pair, 0 means not occupied (absent) and 1 means occupied (present), so for example Hare(1)_Lynx(0) is the number of sites where hare is present, lynx is absent.

When I look here I see the highest number of sites are when both species are absent, followed by hare present lynx absent and both species are present.
To me, this is a strong indication for lynx being dependent on hare.

However, I also calculated Species Interaction Factor (SIF), formula taken from Richmond et al., 2010, and I am struggling to interpret that since we modeled the effects of prey presence/absence on predator (so reminder, dominant species would be prey and subordinate would be predator). According to SIF value, if SIF = 1 species co-occurrence is independent from each other, if SIF < 1 subordinate species is less likely to co-occur with dominant species, and if SIF > 1 subordinate species is more likely to co-occur with dominant species. Here is my SIF result on lynx-hare pair:

It looks like SIF values are distributed mainly around 0.5 in both seasons, which means predator species (lynx) is less likely to co-occur with prey species (hare).
I am struggling to interpret that, because does this mean lynx avoids hare? Or can I say from here hare avoids lynx or is it too much speculation?
Another thing is from my dataset lynx detections are super-low anyway because the population is not so big and they are pretty shy. So maybe because their occupancy would be low anyway due to my spare data on them, is that what I am seeing here?
Or overall am I missing something?

Sorry for the long post, but any help would be appreciated!
I tried to explain things clearly but if something is confusing please ask.
Looking forward to your comments!
Thank you so much!

Best,
Dilsad

--
A. Dilsad Dagtekin
PhD Student at Population Ecology Research Group
University of Zurich, Department of Evolutionary Biology and Environmental Studies
dilsad....@ieu.uzh.ch | www.popecol.org <http://www.popecol.org>
Ecology and Evol. Biology Society of Turkey: www.ekoevo.org <http://www.ekoevo.org>

messages.subject: Non-nested sampling design in multi-scale occupancy model (?)
messages.subject_clean: Non-nested sampling design in multi-scale occupancy model (?)
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone:

I am a little bit new with hierarchical models and I have a special interest with multi-scale occupancy models. I have a question that I hope some of you could help me to answer. Can I use a multi-scale occupancy model even though my data is not nested?

I am doing this question because I have data of covariates collected at different spatial scales and when I define the area of my "sites" I am obligated to dicard some of these covariates. For example, one of my variables was canopy closure calculated in a 10m area surrounding a camera trap, if a define my "site" as a 250m grid around the camera trap, I will not be able to use canopy closure as a covariate. I do not know if is possible that I can use a multi-scale occupancy model to estimte the probability of occurrence at a scale of 10m around camera traps, and the prob of occurrence in grids of 250m (using other covariates) without having nested data.

Unfortunately multi-scale occupancy models haven´t been very widespread in the literature and I haven´t been able to find an answer to this question. I would appreciate if any of you could give me an answer or some advice.

Thank you so much and I apologize in advance if my english is not the best.

   lambda[t] <- Ntot[t+1] / Ntot[t]
   }

#-------------------------------------------------

# 3.1. Likelihood for population population count data (state-space model)
   # 3.1.1 System process
   for (t in 2:nyears){
      mean1[t] <- f[t-1] / 2 * sjuv[t-1] * Ntot[t-1]
      N1[t] ~ dpois(mean1[t])
      Nad[t] ~ dbin(sad[t-1], Ntot[t-1])
      }

      Ntot[t] <- Nad[t] + N1[t]
      }

   for (t in 1:nyears){
      y[t] ~ dnorm(Ntot[t], tauy)

   m[t,1:nyears] ~ dmulti(pr[t,], r[t])
   }

# m-array cell probabilities for juveniles
for (t in 1:(nyears-1)){

      } #j
   # Below main diagonal
   for (j in 1:(t-1)){
      pr[t,j] <- 0
      } #j
   # Last column: probability of non-recapture
   pr[t,nyears] <- 1-sum(pr[t,1:(nyears-1)])
   } #t

# m-array cell probabilities for adults
for (t in 1:(nyears-1)){
   # Main diagonal
   pr[t+nyears-1,t] <- sad[t] * p[t]
   # Above main diagonal
   for (j in (t+1):(nyears-1)){
      pr[t+nyears-1,j] <- prod(sad[t:j])*prod(q[t:(j-1)])*p[j]
      } #j
   # Below main diagonal
   for (j in 1:(t-1)){
      pr[t+nyears-1,j] <- 0
      } #j

   }

# 3. The likelihoods of the single data sets

# 3.1. Likelihood for population population count data (state-space model)
   # 3.1.1 System process
   for (t in 2:nyears){
      mean1[t] <- f[t-1] / 2 * sjuv[t-1] * Ntot[t-1]
      N1[t] ~ dpois(mean1[t])
      Nad[t] ~ dbin(sad[t-1], Ntot[t-1])
      }

      }

   for (t in 1:nyears){

      }

   }

# m-array cell probabilities for juveniles

   # Above main diagonal
   for (j in (t+1):(nyears-1)){
      pr[t,j] <- sjuv[t]*prod(sad[(t+1):j])*prod(q[t:(j-1)])*p[j]
      } #j
   # Below main diagonal
   for (j in 1:(t-1)){
      pr[t,j] <- 0
      } #j
   # Last column: probability of non-recapture
   pr[t,nyears] <- 1-sum(pr[t,1:(nyears-1)])
   } #t

# m-array cell probabilities for adults
for (t in 1:(nyears-1)){
   # Main diagonal
   pr[t+nyears-1,t] <- sad[t] * p[t]
   # Above main diagonal

      } #j
   # Below main diagonal
   for (j in 1:(t-1)){
      pr[t+nyears-1,j] <- 0
      } #j
   # Last column
   pr[t+nyears-1,nyears] <- 1 - sum(pr[t+nyears-1,1:(nyears-1)])
